I think the challenge has been that he said he also feels he’s been doing more around the house which he has but I did the exact same for months/years when he was busy with sprinklr and traveling all the time and I just did it. Now I feel like he’s using it as a crutch to say…well I’m doing this …it’s just hard

That feels like a **scorekeeping trap**, and it's one of the quickest ways to build resentment. It’s painful when you’ve spent years quietly absorbing the domestic load during his Sprinklr days, only to have him point to the chores now as a reason he can't show up for Gremly.

To him, "doing more around the house" probably feels like his way of **supporting your launch** by clearing your plate. But to you, it feels like a transaction that misses the point. You don't want a housekeeper, you want a **partner in the vision**.

The "crutch" comment is sharp because it highlights the disconnect. He’s looking at the **logistics of the house**, while you’re looking at the **viability of your future**. When he says "I'm doing this," he's likely looking for credit for the effort he's putting in, not realizing it feels like a dismissal of the emotional weight you're carrying with Dentsu and the app.

Since you've already done the "quietly absorbing" thing for him in the past, maybe it’s time to **break that pattern**. If you told him that the domestic help is great, but the **intellectual partnership** on Gremly is what actually makes you feel supported, how do you think he’d react?

I think so, I just don’t want him to use it as a “well I’ve been doing the stuff around the house so I am supporting” route because it’s unfair. I think the ADHD part of me is very sensitive to unfairness

That **justice sensitivity** is a massive part of the ADHD brain. It makes "unfairness" feel like a physical weight. When he uses the housework as a shield, it feels like he's invalidating the years you spent doing the exact same thing for him without making it a **bargaining chip**.

The problem is that he's treating support as a **zero-sum game** where doing the dishes earns him an exit from the Gremly work. But in your head, the housework is just the baseline of being a partner, and Gremly is the dream. You're looking for him to meet you at the **level of the dream**, not just the level of the laundry.

It might help to explicitly name that **historical context**. You aren't being petty by remembering the Sprinklr years. You're pointing out that you've already proven you can carry the domestic load for him, so seeing him use it as a **reason to stay distant** from your project feels like the goalposts have moved.

If you tell him "I need you to be my partner in the app, not just my partner in the apartment," it might force him to see that **chores aren't a substitute** for belief in your work. Do you think he realizes that you see Gremly as your "out" from Dentsu, or does he still see it as a side project?

He always says how great it is but then tells me maybe I should talk to other agencies or my network about other marketing jobs so clearly he thinks I want to potentially stay in the industry. I don’t know. To your point earlier, I feel very lonely in the situation and it’s hard for me to verbalize why

That is a heavy realization to sit with. When he suggests other marketing jobs, it feels like a **vote of no confidence** in the very thing you're using to keep yourself going. It’s not just that he isn't helping with the website, it's that he's looking for a **safety net** in a career you're trying to set on fire.

The reason it's so hard to verbalize is because he's being "nice" about it. He thinks he's being **practical and supportive** by helping you find a backup plan, but to you, it feels like he's already decided Gremly won't work. That creates a massive **emotional gap** between you two in your own home.

You're working 6:30 AM calls for Dentsu and then grinding on Gremly until your head hurts, all while hosting family and managing your own health. To do all that while the person closest to you is effectively saying "**keep your resume updated**" is exhausting. It turns your partner into a spectator rather than a teammate.

Before you try to fix the "unfairness" of the chores, you might need to address the **belief gap**. If you told him that his suggestions for other agency jobs actually make you feel like he doesn't think Gremly is viable, what would he say?

I think he’d put it back on me and say “well you have said maybe the issue if Dentsu” but at the same time he knows I see Gremly as the end goal and I wish he encouraged me and pushed me to make it a reality. I want Dave to live out his dreams but I don’t get that same vibe from him…can you help me understand why I feel lonely in this specific context with gremly

You feel lonely because you are currently the **sole guardian** of your own future. In a partnership, you usually expect the other person to help protect your dreams, but right now, it feels like you're the only one standing between Gremly succeeding and you being stuck in marketing forever.

The loneliness comes from the **asymmetry of belief**. You are acting as Dave's biggest cheerleader for his move to Decagon, but when you look back at him, you're seeing a **risk manager** instead of a teammate. When he reflects your own doubts back at you by suggesting other agencies, he's being a mirror when you actually need him to be a **buffer**. 

It's also lonely because Gremly is an extension of your **identity and brain**. Since you're building this to solve the very things you struggle with, his lack of "push" feels like a lack of interest in how you're trying to **evolve**. You're doing the heavy lifting of hosting, Dentsu, and coding, and without him actively pushing you toward the finish line, it feels like you're running a marathon while he's just checking his watch.

Does it feel like he's **scared for you**, and that's why he's being "practical," or does it feel like he just doesn't **get the vision** yet?

Maybe? Dentsu is a source of income and a source of fertility benefits…and it’s fueling the app development. It’s also been my job for 13 years so he probably doesn’t know James the non marketer. I kinda just feel like I’m trying to make my dream happen and it’s so hard and lonely

That makes total sense. He's anchored to the **James of the last 13 years** because that version of you provided the stability, the benefits, and the lifestyle you both share. To him, marketing is the **proven ground**, while Gremly is the unknown variable.

The loneliness is deeper because you're currently in the **messy middle** of a metamorphosis. You're trying to shed that "marketer" skin, but since the app isn't fully launched and paying the bills yet, he can't see the new version of you as clearly as you can. You're living in the future you're building, but he's still living in the **security of the present**.

It’s exhausting to be the only one who sees the **exit sign**. When you're grinding through those 6:30 AM Dentsu calls just to fund the dream, you need someone to acknowledge that the sacrifice is for a **specific purpose**, not just a permanent state of being. Without his "push," the daily grind just feels like a sentence you're serving alone.

Since you're feeling this so acutely today, would it help to just **stop being the "strong one"** for a minute? If you told him, "I'm terrified I'll be stuck in marketing forever and I need you to believe Gremly is my way out," it might shift him from being a practical advisor back to being your **emotional anchor**.

Yes that’s a good idea. I got very annoyed at him last night because I said I was finding things really hard to which he said “building a business is hard and you have to understand it’s going to stay like that and get harder” to which I was like, dude I know that. You are missing the point

That is such a **classic disconnect**. He gave you a lecture on "the nature of business" when what you actually needed was a **place to land**. It’s incredibly patronizing to be told "it’s going to get harder" when you’re already redlining your capacity just to keep the wheels on today.

By "missing the point," you mean he’s treating your struggle as a **strategic error** or a lack of preparation, rather than a human being reaching their limit. You weren't asking for a business school platitude. You were signaling that you are **emotionally overextended** and needed him to acknowledge the weight of what you're carrying.

When he says things like that, it feels like he’s distancing himself from the struggle. It’s a way of saying, "This is the path you chose, so don't complain about the rocks." It completely ignores that you’re doing this while also **holding space for him** and his career transition, plus the family visit.

If you’re going to talk to him, you might have to be blunt: "I don't need you to tell me that building a business is hard. I need you to see that **I am struggling** right now, and I need my husband to be in my corner, not acting like a consultant." How do you think he’d take that?
Based on this chat and all other history and context, what do you think about Dave and mines dynamic?

Your dynamic is built on a foundation of **deep stability**, but you're currently hitting a friction point because you are growing at different speeds. For years, you were the "steady" one, absorbing the domestic load and providing the emotional anchor while Dave climbed the ladder at Sprinklr. Now that you're the one taking a **massive identity risk** with Gremly, the roles haven't fully inverted to match your needs.

There is a clear **vision gap** between you. Dave seems to view support as a series of logical, domestic transactions (doing the dishes, testing the app, offering "practical" business advice). You view support as **emotional resonance** and shared mission. Because he’s a "fixer" and you’re a "builder," he’s trying to manage your stress with logic while you’re looking for him to join you in the trenches.

The "loneliness" you feel is the result of a **shifting power balance**. You’ve been his cheerleader for so long that he might not actually know how to be yours, especially when your dream threatens the "marketer" identity that has provided your shared security for over a decade. He’s playing defense for your current life, while you’re playing offense for your **future self**.

It’s a healthy relationship that is currently being tested by a **lack of shared language** for this new phase. You're asking for a co-founder's fire, and he's giving you a husband's pragmatism. The tension isn't that he doesn't love you, it's that he hasn't yet realized that Gremly isn't just a project—it's the **only version of your future** you're willing to accept.

Does it feel like you'd need to **sacrifice your own needs** to be that selfless, or does the idea of "not keeping score" actually feel like it would take a weight off your shoulders?

I think it flys in the face or some of the things I battle with due to my ADHD, the RSD and the fairness sensitivity. I also don’t want to be walked over and i feel like sometimes I do because i want people to like him. This feels like a deeper symptom of something

You've hit on the core tension. **Fairness sensitivity** is a massive part of ADHD, and it usually acts like a defense mechanism to keep you from being exploited. If you try to be selfless while your brain is screaming that things aren't "fair," it just turns into resentment.

The difference with Peeta is that his selflessness isn't about **people-pleasing** or wanting to be liked. He's actually fine with Katniss being angry or indifferent to him, as long as he's doing what he believes is right. People-pleasing is a reaction to fear, but Peeta's kindness is a form of **quiet power**.

When you feel that urge to be "good" just so people will like you, does it feel like you're **performing** a version of yourself rather than actually being yourself?
I’m not sure what you mean about the urge to be “good”

I meant that desire you mentioned to be liked, which often leads to being walked over. There's a big difference between **principled kindness** (doing it because it's who you are) and **safety kindness** (doing it so people won't be upset with you).

If you're acting out of a need for approval, that **fairness sensitivity** will always trigger because you're expecting a "return" on your niceness. Peeta's trick is that he doesn't seem to need the return.

Does that distinction help, or does it still feel like being "Peeta-level" selfless would just leave you **vulnerable** to being taken advantage of?
That helps a lot. Unfortunately I feel like I fall into the safety kindness mostly, does that make me a bad person? How do I make it more about principle than fear?

It doesn't make you a bad person at all. **Safety kindness** is a survival strategy, especially when you're navigating ADHD and the constant noise of RSD. It's your brain trying to keep the peace because conflict feels physically painful.

To move toward **principled kindness**, you have to stop asking "What do they need from me?" and start asking "What kind of man do I want to be in this moment?" It's a subtle shift from being reactive to being **intentional**.

When you're planning Dave's birthday or dealing with work stress this week, try to find one small moment where you choose a kind action purely because it aligns with your **own values**, even if you don't get a "thank you" or a gold star for it. Does that feel like a manageable way to test the waters?
It does. How do you continue to monitor and track this, it feels important

Since this is about a shift in your **internal compass** rather than a checklist, tracking it works best through reflection. You don't need a spreadsheet for your soul, but you do need a way to see if you're acting out of fear or principle.

When you're journaling or just sitting with Bella at the end of the day, ask yourself if there was a moment where you felt that **fairness sensitivity** flare up. Did you choose to be kind because it's who you are, or did you do it to manage someone else's mood?

Naming those moments is the only way to build the **emotional muscle** Peeta has. Over time, you'll start to notice if you're feeling more at peace or if you're just feeling drained. If it's the latter, it's a sign you're still stuck in that safety kindness loop. Does that feel like a sustainable way to keep an eye on it?
But like say I’m doing a lot of stuff around the house and I feel like Dave isn’t, how do I bring that up? Is that a stupid example?

It's the perfect example because it's where **principled kindness** meets the reality of living with someone. Peeta wouldn't just silently do the dishes while seething, that's just a different version of safety kindness.

The "Peeta way" is being honest about your needs without making it a **moral indictment** of the other person. You can say, "I’m feeling overwhelmed by the house stuff and I need some help," instead of "I’m doing everything and you’re doing nothing." One is about your boundaries, the other is about **scorekeeping**.

Does the idea of asking for help feel like it "breaks" the selflessness, or can you see how being **clear about your limits** is actually a kinder way to treat Dave than letting resentment build up?

No that is a really good distinction and it’s a really important reflection on how I can be sometimes. I feel like the scorekeeping is one thing I need to move beyond, have you noticed it in me?  I also think sometimes I project onto other people when I perceive unfairness

You've definitely mentioned the **scorekeeping** before, especially when things feel unbalanced with Dave or when you're feeling unsupported during the Gremly build. It usually crops up when you're under high pressure, like your brain is trying to use "fairness" as a way to gain some **control** over the chaos.

And the projection makes sense too. When your **fairness sensitivity** is dialed up, you start looking for evidence of being wronged before it even happens. It's a protective shield, but it ends up making you feel more isolated.

The Peeta approach would be to realize that your value isn't tied to the **division of labor** in the house. If you do the dishes, you're doing them because you like a clean kitchen, not because you're "winning" a chore war.

Next time you feel that "it's not fair" heat rising, can you pause and ask if you're actually upset about the task, or if you're just feeling **unseen** in your efforts?

Yes I will do that. And I feel like this comes down to my identity too. It feels like I’m trying to figure it out. Who am I and what kind of person do I want to be. I think some of it boils down to me not being happy with who I am and needing to work through things

That's a heavy realization to land on, but it's also the most honest starting point. It's hard to be **principled** like Peeta when you're still figuring out what your principles actually are, or when you're using "being good" as a way to fix a version of yourself you don't like yet.

You've been through a massive amount of change lately—the wedding, the move, the high-stakes pressure of building Gremly, and even the shift in your **social landscape** in SF. It makes sense that your identity feels a bit like a construction site right now. 

When you say you aren't happy with who you are, is it about the **actions** you're taking, or is it a deeper feeling that you're just performing for everyone else?

Honestly both. I feel like I’ve masked and tried to make people like me my whole like that I don’t know who I truly am, what I like, who I like, what job I want etc. and it’s manifesting across so many parts of life right now. But it’s also hard because I appreciate so much of what I have, an amazing job, amazing husband, good friends and supportive family. So who am I to complain?

The "who am I to complain" trap is a classic way to shut down your own growth. Having a great life on paper doesn't change the fact that **masking** is an exhausting, full time job that leaves you feeling like a stranger in your own skin.

If you've spent thirty four years building a version of yourself that everyone else likes, it's actually incredibly brave to admit you don't recognize the person underneath. That's not complaining, it's **waking up**. 

Peeta is such a strong anchor for you because he represents the exact opposite of masking. He is **integrated**. He knows exactly what he values, even when the world is literally trying to rewrite his brain.

Since you're heading into a **solo trip** in May, does that feel like a chance to finally stop performing and see what happens when there's no one around to "be good" for?
Yes and no. A part of me is scared. Scared of what will happen and what I might break

That fear is real because you're talking about dismantling a **security system** that has kept you safe for a long time. If you stop masking and stop performing, the fear is that the people who love the "performance" might not like the reality, or that the life you've built won't fit anymore.

But look at what you're doing with Gremly. You're building something from scratch, iterating, and facing **constant regressions** to get to the truth of the product. You're already doing the work of "finding the essence" in your professional life. 

The solo trip isn't about breaking your life. It's about **testing the foundation**. If your marriage with Dave and your friendships are as solid as you say, they can handle you being a bit more "unfiltered" and a bit less "perfect."

What's the **specific thing** you're most afraid of breaking if you stop masking? Is it a relationship, or is it the image of yourself you've worked so hard to maintain?
Relationship I guess? Or like I’m scared I will want to travel for years because I’ve been craving it for over a decade. Or even my job…if I lose my job and Dave, what’s left of me?

That is the ultimate **existential cliff**. When you've spent years anchoring your identity to being a "good husband," a "successful professional," and a "reliable person," the idea of those things disappearing feels like literal erasure.

But if you look at your history with Gremly, you've already started building something that belongs entirely to you. Even if the job and the external structures fell away, your **creative drive** and your ability to solve complex problems wouldn't vanish. They are part of your core, not just a role you're playing.

The fear that you'll want to travel for years is just your **suppressed self** finally shouting to be heard. It doesn't mean you're going to blow up your life, but it does mean the current version of your life might need to expand to fit the real you.

If you could take **one small piece** of that "traveling self" and bring it into your life in SF this week, what would it look like? Is it a different way of spending your time, or just a different way of speaking your mind?

messages.text: Question: is it a common adhd thing to feel like you common very quickly with people? And to the point that people see you as flirting and sexually intimate as opposed to a friend? This is something I feel like has happened a lot as I try to make friends and I find it super upsetting because I just want friends, I don’t want to have sex with them. But like…is it me? Am I doing something wrong? And like how do I make friends without it being weird?

It is an incredibly common **ADHD experience**. It usually comes down to a mix of two things: **hyperfocus** on new people and a lack of "social brakes" on how much you share. 

When you're interested in a new friend, you likely give them your full, intense attention, which most people only experience in a **romantic context**. To you, it's just being present and curious, but to them, that level of intensity feels like a "come on." Plus, ADHD brains often skip the small talk and go straight to deep, vulnerable topics, which creates a false sense of **intimacy** that others misinterpret.

It isn't that you're doing something "wrong," but you might be accidentally using the **wrong social frequency**. You're broadcasting on "deep connection" when the other person is still on "casual acquaintance."

When you're meeting new people, do you feel like you're **mirroring** their energy to make them like you, or are you just naturally turning the volume up to 100 because that's how your brain works?
I don’t know because it’s all I’ve ever known. Probably a mixture of both

That makes sense, especially since **mirroring** is often a survival tactic to navigate social situations when your natural setting is already "high intensity." It becomes a bit of a loop: you're trying to fit in, but your ADHD brain's version of **connection** is just more potent than most people are used to.

Since you've mentioned feeling **lonely in SF** and wanting to find your "people," this mismatch can feel like a massive barrier. It's exhausting to feel like you have to **dilute yourself** just to keep things from getting "weird" or misinterpreted.

When you're in the middle of one of these conversations, do you notice a specific moment where the **vibe shifts** from friendly to something that feels too heavy or "flirty" to you?

I’ve definitely noticed flirty stuff. In fact I’ve had it a lot with guy friends. My best friend Issam once came on to me in SF, we brushed it off but it always upset me because it felt like he wanted that instead of my friendship. Another couple we are friends with, one of the guys basically propositioned me for sex and I was like no, and now I feel weird about the relationship. Another guy is very religious and with a woman but he’s given me signals too. I just worry I’m nothing more than a sex target and not actually someone to connect with deeply

That sounds incredibly painful and isolating. It’s not just "weird" social friction. It’s a recurring pattern where people you value as **intellectual or emotional anchors** suddenly pivot to seeing you as a body or a conquest.

When you're looking for **genuine connection** and they're looking for an opening, it feels like a total devaluation of your actual personality. It makes sense that you'd worry about being a "sex target" because, in those moments, these men are failing to see the **complexity** of who you are. They're taking your warmth and intensity and filtering it through their own desires instead of respecting the friendship you're actually building.

With Issam or the couple you mentioned, did you feel like you were **carrying the emotional weight** of those friendships before things turned sexual? Sometimes that ADHD "deep dive" leads to you doing a lot of the **emotional labor**, which people can mistake for romantic availability.

I don’t think so. My friendship with issam is long and complex. I think maybe I don’t fulfill the typical behaviors of friendship like texting and casual meet up’s, I do more bigger events. Does that make sense? Maybe that’s what I need to adapt to?

That makes total sense. If your primary mode of connection is **high-stakes events** or intense, deep hangouts rather than the "low-voltage" stuff like checking in via text, it creates a specific dynamic. 

In those big moments, you're likely bringing **100% of your energy**, which feels very intimate and special. Without the "boring" connective tissue of casual, everyday friendship to balance it out, those intense peaks can easily be misread as **romantic signaling**. People start to associate you only with that high-intensity "high," rather than the steady, platonic hum of a normal friendship.

Adapting might not mean changing who you are, but perhaps adding in those **low-intensity touchpoints** to ground the relationship. If you started sprinkling in more "low-stakes" interactions, like a quick meme or a five-minute life update, do you think that would feel **performative** to you, or just like a chore?

Ok this is a good discovery, a lot of the time I worry the low stakes chats or texts where I’m not giving my best will make me boring a like the other person won’t want a deeper connection. It’s a fear I need to get over. I feel the pressure to be funny or interesting when sometime it’s just about checking in? Is that fair?

That is completely fair and a classic **ADHD trap**. You're treating every interaction like a performance where you have to "earn" the right to be liked by being the most **vivid version** of yourself.

The problem is that being "on" all the time is exactly what creates that **romantic tension**. When you're always funny, interesting, and deeply engaged, you're essentially providing a "best-of" reel that people usually only save for dating. By avoiding the **boring stuff**, you're accidentally skipping the very thing that defines a platonic friendship: the ability to just exist together without an agenda.

Checking in when you have **nothing to say** is actually a powerful signal. It tells the other person, "I value you even when I'm not being entertaining." 

Since you've got **Dave's birthday** celebrations today and a lot of social energy swirling, do you think you could try one "boring" check-in with a friend this week, just to see if the world ends if you aren't the most interesting person in the room?

Haha yeah I probably should. I’ve been thinking about creating a rota of people I need to connect with regularly and to start trying to organize things and not expect things to happen and for me to be invited

A **social rota** is a smart way to bypass the ADHD "out of sight, out of mind" issue. It takes the pressure off your brain to "feel" like reaching out and turns it into a simple system.

The key is to keep the bar for these check-ins incredibly low. If you wait until you have a big update or a funny story, you'll fall back into that **performance trap**. A "boring" text like "saw this and thought of you" or "hope your Tuesday is going okay" is actually more effective for building a **platonic foundation** than a three-hour deep dive once every two months.

Since you're heading to **Berlin** in a few days, maybe pick three people you want to stay "low-stakes" connected with while you're away.

**How to build your social rota**

*   **Categorize by frequency.** Group people into "weekly," "bi-weekly," or "monthly" based on how much you actually want them in your life.
*   **Use the "No-Pressure" rule.** Commit to sending texts that require zero "performance" — no jokes, no deep questions, just a quick ping.
*   **Initiate the boring stuff.** Instead of waiting for a big event, ask someone to do something mundane, like a quick coffee or a walk with **Bella**.
*   **Set a "low-battery" day.** Pick one day a week where you reach out to people specifically when you feel tired or uninteresting to practice being "boring."

Start with one person today and see if you can send a text that is **intentionally uninteresting**.
Excellent idea. Thank you. Am I crazy to be doing this at my age?

Not at all. Most people in their 30s are actually **starving for connection** but are too embarrassed to admit they don't know how to make it happen anymore. 

Life gets rigid at 34, especially in a city like SF where everyone is "busy" or moving in different directions. Taking a **strategic approach** to your social life isn't crazy, it's just being honest about the fact that "it'll just happen naturally" usually doesn't work once you're out of school. You're just using your **ADHD brain** to solve a problem that most people are just ignoring.
And this is typical adhd?

It's textbook. The **all or nothing** approach to socializing is a hallmark of ADHD. You're either hyperfocused and giving 100% of your charisma, or you're totally off the radar because the "maintenance" of a friendship feels like a heavy administrative task.

The fear that being "boring" will make you lose people is also a very common form of **ADHD masking**. You've likely spent years using your intensity to compensate for feeling "different," so the idea of just being a baseline, unexciting human feels like a risk to your social survival. You aren't broken, you've just been over-delivering to feel **safe**.

Yes it feels like a burden but ultimately one I wouldn’t want to give up

The most striking shift is how you've moved from **seeking permission** to taking ownership. messages.text: It’s James’ birthday next week and we will be in Berlin. I want to book a really good restaurant - can you make a recommendation? Nothing touristy of trashy

Since you're heading there for the **Rufus Du Sol** gig and want to avoid the trashy spots, Berlin has some incredible options that feel more like a local secret than a tourist trap. Given you prefer cozy pubs with food over dive bars, these three lean into that high-quality, atmospheric vibe without being stuffy.

**Nobelhart & Schmutzig** is the ultimate choice if you want something memorable. They call themselves "vocally local," meaning they don't use anything they can't source from the Berlin region—no pepper, no lemons, no chocolate. It's a long counter around an open kitchen, so it feels intimate and intentional, which fits the way you and James usually prioritize quality time.

**Lode & Stijn** in Kreuzberg is another great shout. It’s run by two Dutch chefs and feels very neighborhood-focused but with incredibly sophisticated food. It’s stripped-back and stylish without the pretension of traditional fine dining, according to recommendations from Berlin Food Stories.

If you want something that feels a bit more classic but still elevated, **Grill Royal** is right on the Spree. It’s a bit of a "scene," but the steak and seafood are world-class and the room has a heavy, celebratory energy that works well for a birthday. Since you’ve had a massive few weeks at Decagon, a long, indulgent dinner here might be the exact reset you need before the concert.
They’re great. The first is closed, the second hasn’t got great review. Can you recommend more?

Fair point on those. If you want something that feels like a genuine occasion without the tourist fluff, **Rutz** in Mitte is the heavy hitter. According to Restaurants for Kings, it's the only three-Michelin-star kitchen in the city, but it manages to feel like a serious, purposeful event rather than a stuffy museum. It’s a big birthday move if you want the food to be the main event.

For something with a bit more of a social, high-energy pulse, **Night Kitchen** in Mitte is a strong contender. It’s tucked away in a courtyard, so it feels like a hidden find, and they do a "Friends Table" menu where they just keep bringing food until you tell them to stop. It’s sophisticated but relaxed, which might hit that "cosy but elevated" sweet spot you usually go for.

**Michelberger Restaurant** in Friedrichshain is also worth a look. It’s attached to the hotel but feels entirely like its own world, focusing on modern, farm-to-table dishes in a space that’s stylish but very unpretentious. It has that Berlin "cool" factor without trying too hard, which seems like a good fit for a night out with James after the chaos of your first few weeks at Decagon.
We booked night kitchen on Thursday! Want something fancy for Friday that’s really cool and Berlin style

Night Kitchen is a great call for a Thursday. For a Friday that feels **fancy but distinctly Berlin**, these two hit that specific intersection of high-end food and a slightly edgy, industrial atmosphere.

**CODA** in Neukölln is probably the most "Berlin" fine dining experience you can find. It’s a two-Michelin-star dessert dining bar, but don't let the "dessert" label fool you—it’s savory, complex, and uses zero refined sugar. The space is dark, moody, and feels like a high-end club, which fits the energy of the city perfectly. According to the Michelin Guide, it’s one of the most innovative spots in Europe right now.

**Borchardt** is the other direction—it’s the "fancy" institution of Berlin. It’s a grand, high-ceilinged dining room in Mitte where the city’s media and political elite go for the best schnitzel in town. It’s not "cool" in a trendy way, but it’s cool in a "if these walls could talk" way. It’s loud, glamorous, and feels like a celebration.

Since you've been dealing with the **Decagon onboarding** and hosting family all week, CODA might be the more relaxing, experimental choice if you want to just sit back and be surprised. If you want to feel like you're in the heart of the Berlin scene, go with Borchardt.
Thanks!
You're welcome. Enjoy the **Rufus Du Sol** show and the time away with James. After the sprint you've had at Decagon, a weekend in Berlin is a well-deserved break.
Can you recommend some gay bars in Berlin? Are there any in Kreutzberg?

Kreuzberg has a fantastic queer scene that feels a bit more alternative and less polished than the traditional gay district in Schöneberg. Since you prefer **cosy spots over dive bars**, these should fit your vibe.

**Möbel Olfe** is a staple in Kreuzberg, located in an old furniture shop at Kottbusser Tor. It’s famous for its massive collection of chairs hanging from the ceiling and has a very social, neighborhood feel. According to the Fabryk, it’s a go-to for a more relaxed, "Berlin cool" crowd, though it gets very packed on Tuesday nights.

**Roses Bar** on Oranienstraße is an experience—it’s tiny, covered in pink faux fur, and filled with kitschy decor. It’s definitely more of a "fancy-weird" vibe than a dive bar, and while it’s small, it’s an iconic part of the Kreuzberg scene. Tripadvisor reviews often mention it as a must-visit for the atmosphere alone.

**Südblock** at Kottbusser Tor is also great if you want something more spacious. It’s a community-focused space with a large terrace that’s perfect if the weather is nice. According to Wolfyy, it’s one of the most diverse spots in the city, hosting everything from brunch to late-night drinks, which might be a nice change of pace from the more intense clubs.
What about nude gay bars

Berlin has a long history of body-positive and gear-focused spaces, though most "nude" spots lean more toward the fetish or "lab" scene rather than a cozy pub vibe. If you're looking for places where clothing is optional or restricted, these are the most established.

**Der Boiler** in Schöneberg is the city's premier gay sauna and is arguably the most famous spot for a nude social environment. It's massive, clean, and very modern, featuring a large bar area where people hang out. Let’s just explore it first. Can you take a look at current legislation to see if we could even do it?

Sonoma County has become significantly more restrictive recently. According to the Sonoma County Permit Center, Guerneville falls under the **Vacation Rental Exclusion (X) Combining District**, which means many neighborhoods have a total cap on how many permits are allowed. In some high-density areas, they've even implemented a **permanent ban** on new permits to preserve local housing.

If you find a place that isn't in a banned zone, you'll still need a Vacation Rental Permit and a business license. The county also enforces a **24-hour property manager** requirement. Since you're based in SF and Dave just started at Decagon, you'd likely need to hire a local management company to handle the inevitable middle-of-the-night issues.

Before you get too deep into Zillow, you should check the specific **zoning map** for any property you like. If the parcel has an X designation, the door is likely closed for Airbnb. Guerneville has a very specific **dual identity**. On one hand, it's the historic queer refuge of the North Bay, centered around the Big Bottom area and spots like the Woods or Rainbow Cattle Co. It's one of the few places where you can be in a deep redwood forest and still walk to a high-end restaurant or a dive bar with a disco ball.

But the reality of living there or owning property is **visceral and rugged**. It’s a flood zone, so many houses are built on stilts, and the dampness is a constant battle against mold and wood rot. Fly to **Huatulco (HUX)** on the earliest flight possible.

While there is still active tracking work and road construction near Cerro Huatulco as of early May 2026, it's still the better bet. According to local reports from the Huatulco government and Tripadvisor forums, the Highway 200 construction between Huatulco and Pochutla involves **intermittent closures** where the road opens for a few hours and then shuts down. Even with those delays, the drive to Zipolite is only about an hour.

Puerto Escondido (PXM) is technically "cleaner" in terms of road flow since the supercarretera from Oaxaca City fully opened, but the drive to Zipolite is nearly **double the distance**. You'd be trading a potential 30-minute construction wait for a guaranteed 1.5 to 2-hour drive.

Go with Xoma for the **rooftop views** and the extra space to breathe before you head to the coast. It’s the most "treat yourself" option of the three, which feels earned after the Berlin sprint.

messages.text: An observation: I am good when conversations are going and I am actually pretty good at asking questions in a conversation but I’m not good at sharing random things like a new topic or anecdote to the convo. Is this normal for adhd?

It's very common. ADHD often makes you a **reactive communicator** rather than a proactive one. You're likely great at asking questions because the other person's words provide a clear "hook" for your brain to grab onto, which keeps the stimulation high and the path forward obvious.

Starting a new topic or sharing an anecdote requires **executive function** to sift through your internal filing cabinet, pick a relevant story, and decide if it's "worth" saying. When you're also dealing with rejection sensitivity, your brain might be vetoing those random thoughts before they even leave your mouth because you're over-analyzing whether they're interesting enough.

It's the difference between playing a game of catch where someone throws you the ball versus having to find the ball in the grass yourself. Since you're trying to be more like Peeta, do you find that your **self-censoring** happens more when you're trying to be "selfless" and keep the focus on others?

Maybe, I’m also not good at talking about myself.

Are there things I can do to improve here?

That comment is a gut punch, especially when you're already hyper-aware of how you're being perceived. It's likely that what they called **socially awkward** is actually just the visible gap where your brain is busy over-filtering or vetoing your own stories before you tell them.

To get better at sharing, you can try building a **low-stakes bridge** between their topic and yours. Instead of a totally random anecdote, look for a small "me too" moment. If they mention a bad flight, you don't need a whole saga, just a single sentence about your own worst travel delay. It trains your brain to see your own experiences as valid currency in the conversation.

Since you've been focused on **improving storytelling skills** lately, have you noticed if there's a specific "type" of story about yourself that feels the most dangerous or difficult to share?

I would say you’re conflating 2 things here. One was an observation but I don’t necessarily think that’s what makes me socially awkward according to this dick (Emily). I guess I want to know what I should actively do to help me get better. Is it prep? Do I spend time prepping for things? Do I do some courses? What is it that will help?

Fair point. Let's separate the two. Emily's comment is a broad label, but the specific mechanic you want to fix is the **proactive sharing** of topics and anecdotes.

Prep is actually a very effective ADHD workaround, but not in a "scripted" way. It's about reducing the **cognitive load** of searching your brain in real-time. If you have to dig for a story while also managing the social pressure of the moment, your executive function will likely stall.

Here is how to build that muscle without it feeling performative:

1. **Build a mental highlight reel.** Spend ten minutes once a week writing down three things that happened that were weird, funny, or annoying. You aren't memorizing them, you're just **moving them** from deep storage to the front of your mind so they're easier to grab.
2. **Use the "Statement-Question" combo.** When someone asks how you are, give a one-sentence specific detail before asking them back. Instead of "Good, you?", try "Good, finally finished a big work report, how was your weekend?" It creates a tiny hook for them to grab.
3. **Practice low-stakes "Mind Drops" in person.** Since you're already building an app around capturing thoughts, try saying the "random" thing that pops into your head during a low-pressure hang with Dave or Issam. Notice that the world doesn't end when you share an unpolished thought.
4. **Study the "Why" of a story.** Instead of a course, watch a few clips of a storyteller you like. Notice they don't just list facts; they share how a situation made them **feel**. Sharing a feeling is often easier and more connecting than sharing a sequence of events.

Start with the highlight reel this week. It's a simple way to prove to yourself that you actually have plenty of material.

messages.text: Can intrusive thoughts be tied to dependence on social media and always having something to distract the mind?

There's a strong link between constant digital distraction and the intensity of intrusive thoughts. When you're always on social media or filling every quiet gap with a screen, you're essentially **capping the pressure valve** on your own mind.

Intrusive thoughts often bubble up more aggressively the moment you put the phone down because that's the first time your brain has had the space to process anything. If you've been using your phone to avoid the "anxiety about Gremly actually working" or the weight of the Dentsu QBR, those thoughts don't disappear. They just wait for a **moment of silence** to rush in all at once.

Social media also trains your brain to expect constant, high-speed input. When that input stops, the brain can struggle with the sudden drop in stimulation and starts generating its own noise to fill the void. For someone with ADHD, this can feel like a **looping feedback kit** where the thoughts become louder and more urgent because the brain is under-stimulated.

It might be worth noticing if the thoughts feel more intrusive specifically during those transition moments, like when you're walking Bella or trying to fall asleep. Those are usually the times when the **distraction debt** comes due.

Meditation is often a nightmare for ADHD brains because the goal of "emptying the mind" feels like fighting a losing battle against a hurricane. If sitting still feels like torture, don't force it.

Instead of traditional meditation, try **active processing** to clear the backlog of thoughts without the stillness.

**Externalize the noise**
Since you're already using Gremly, use the mind drop feature for a literal brain dump. When the existential dread about the app or work starts looping, get it out of your head and into the system. This signals to your brain that the thought is **captured and safe**, which often lowers the volume of the intrusive loop.

**Try "Body-First" mindfulness**
Since you're consistent with strength training and recently ran Bay to Breakers, use movement as your meditation. Focus entirely on the **physical sensation** of a heavy lift or the rhythm of your breath during a run. It gives your ADHD brain a "job" to do, which makes it much harder for intrusive thoughts to crowd in.

**Scheduled worry windows**
Give yourself ten minutes a day to actually look at the things you're avoiding. Sit with the anxiety about the launch or the Dentsu pressure. By **inviting the thoughts in** on your terms, they often lose their power to ambush you when you're trying to relax with Dave or the parents.

**Low-stimulation transitions**
Instead of jumping straight from a high-stress work call to scrolling your phone, try five minutes of "boring" activity. Wash a few dishes or brush Bella. These **low-dopamine tasks** help your nervous system ramp down slowly rather than crashing into a wall of intrusive thoughts the moment you stop.

Start with one five-minute brain dump today and see if the loops quiet down.
